$comment: MOCK ONLY. Stands in for server-side scoring; never ship keys to the client in production.

final_explain.f1: The trigger starts the execution; the items travel inside it, and every node handles them one by one.
final_explain.f2: The trigger and the middle of the pipeline are already proven by the green runs. The only unknown is what the other system answered — and that is in the last node’s response.
final_explain.f3: Set reshapes, Filter decides. Confusing the two is how data gets “cleaned” by silently dropping it.
final_explain.f4: 300 − 36 − 41 = 223. Move the duplicate guard downstream and the 41 repeats are alerted before anything checks them: 300 − 36 = 264.
final_explain.f5: Success describes the node, not the outcome. The outcome is in the response it got back.
final_explain.f6: The guard compares values exactly. Until case and spacing are made uniform, one address is two different strings.
final_explain.f7: Expressions are per item and on the fly — which is why one misspelled field name fails on every item.
final_explain.f8: Normalise before you compare or default. Otherwise “FREE ” and “free” live side by side as two plans.
final_explain.f9: A guard placed after the action runs, shows green, and protects nothing.
final_explain.f10: Nothing errored: the expression simply found no such field. Quiet failures like this are why field names are tidied once, upstream.
final_explain.f11: A trustworthy pipeline can say how many rows each guard stopped and why — not just that it ran.
final_explain.f12: Two ordering faults at once: nothing protects the write, and the guards compare values that have not been cleaned yet.
